units.title: Expectations
units.intro: Grammar: idiomatic expressions and inversion (So do I, Neither do I, Not only ... but also).

cards.title: Idiomatic expressions
rule: An **idiom** is a group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the separate words: *break the ice* = start a conversation; *a piece of cake* = very easy; *once in a blue moon* = very rarely; *hit the books* = study hard; *under the weather* = slightly ill.
Learn idioms as whole units and from context; don’t translate word by word.

examples.text: The test was a piece of cake.
He is under the weather (= standing outside in the rain).
examples.fix: Under the weather means slightly ill.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: One of the most challenging obstacles facing high school graduates ________ the rising cost of higher education.

steps.text: The subject of the sentence is 'One' (singular) in the pattern $$\text{One of} + \text{Plural Noun} + \text{Singular Verb}$$.
The plural noun phrase 'the most challenging obstacles' is part of a prepositional phrase modifying the subject.
Students often match the verb to the plural noun 'obstacles' which is closest to the verb slot, leading them to choose 'are' (Option A).

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: The board of directors, despite having conflicting opinions on the new expansion policy, ________ finally agreed on the budget.

steps.text: The subject is 'The board' (singular collective noun).
The phrase 'of directors' and the parenthetical clause 'despite having conflicting opinions...' are intervening elements that do not change the subject's singular number.
Students are often distracted by the plural nouns 'directors' and 'opinions' and select the plural auxiliary 'have' (Option B).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Neither the regional program coordinator nor the senior researchers ________ present at the emergency project meeting yesterday.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The compound subject is connected by the correlative conjunction 'Neither... nor'. The proximity rule applies, meaning the verb agrees with the closer subject, 'the senior researchers' (plural).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students may focus on 'the coordinator' (singular) and choose 'was' (Option A). The past time marker 'yesterday' eliminates present auxiliaries 'is' and 'are', leaving 'were' (Option B) as the correct choice.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ምሉእ ሓሳብ ብ 'Neither... nor' ክእሰር ከሎ፡ እቲ ግሲ ምስቲ ናብኡ ዝቐረበ ባእታ ይሰማማዕ (Proximity Rule)። እቲ ዝቐረበ ባእታ 'the senior researchers' (ብዙሕ) ስለ ዝኾነን እቲ ግዜ ድማ 'yesterday' (ትማሊ) ስለ ዝኾነን፡ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'were' (Option B) እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The local police ________ currently searching the forest area for the prisoners who escaped from the regional jail.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
'Police' is a collective noun that is always plural in English and must be paired with plural verbs.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Because 'police' does not end in '-s', students often assume it is singular and choose 'is' (Option A) or 'was' (Option C). The time marker 'currently' indicates present tense, which makes 'are' (Option B) correct.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Police' (ፖሊስ) ዝብል ስም ብቅርጹ ነጸላ ይመስል እምበር፡ ብሰዋስው ወግዒ ግን ወትሩ ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ (plural) እዩ። 'currently' (ኣብዚ እዋን) ዝብል ቃል ድማ ህልው እዋን ስለ ዝሕብር፡ ምስኡ ዝኸይድ ግሲ 'are' (Option B) እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What does "once in a blue moon" mean?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** A "blue moon" is a rare event, so the idiom means very rarely.

**Step 2:** It has nothing to do with the colour of the moon.

**Step 3:** Example: He visits us once in a blue moon.

**Tip:** Idioms have meanings that differ from their separate words. After negative adverbs (never, rarely, not only, hardly) at the start, invert the subject and auxiliary.

cards.title: Inversion
rule: **So / Neither + auxiliary + subject** to agree: *I like music. — **So do I**.* *I can’t swim. — **Neither can I**.* Use the same auxiliary as the first sentence (do/does/did for simple tenses).

After negative words at the start (*Not only, Never, Seldom, Hardly, Rarely*) put the **auxiliary before the subject**: ***Not only did he** pass, **but** he **also** won a prize.* ***Never have I** seen such a crowd.*

examples.text: She passed and so did her brother.
Not only he passed but also...
examples.fix: Not only did he pass, but he also...

examples.text: Seldom do we see snow here.

cards.pattern: So/Neither + aux + S  ·  Not only + aux + S + V, but ... also

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "Not only he passed but also..."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** **So / Neither + auxiliary + subject** to agree: *I like music. — **So do I**.* *I can’t swim. — **Neither can I**.* Use the same auxiliary as the first sentence (do/does/did for simple tenses).
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "Not only he passed but also..." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "Not only did he pass, but he also..."

**Check:** After negative words at the start (*Not only, Never, Seldom, Hardly, Rarely*) put the **auxiliary before the subject**: ***Not only did he** pass, **but** he **also** won a prize.* ***Never have I** seen such a crowd.*

cards.answer: Not only did he pass, but he also...

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Idioms have meanings different from their words and must be learned as units. To agree, use So (positive) or Neither (negative) + auxiliary + subject. After negative words at the start (Not only, Never, Seldom), invert the auxiliary and the subject.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.why: The first clause is negative ('never wastes'). To agree with a negative statement, we can use 'neither + auxiliary + subject' (D) OR 'subject + negative auxiliary + either' (C). Both are correct.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I will not answer a call unless it is my phone. (He)
cards.why: The original sentence is negative ('will not'). To agree with a negative statement, we use 'Neither + auxiliary + subject'. The auxiliary here is 'will'.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The statement is negative ('never wastes').
**Step 2:** For negative additions, we can use two structures:
1. **Neither + Auxiliary + Subject** (Neither does she)
2. **Subject + Auxiliary (negative) + Either** (She doesn't either)
**Step 3:** Since both C and D follow these rules, option E is correct.

glossary.meaning: An expression whose meaning is not the sum of its words.
Putting the auxiliary before the subject.

questions.q: I didn’t see him at school___.
why: The original statement is in the Simple Past negative ('didn't see'). To agree with a negative statement, we use 'Neither' or 'Nor' followed by the auxiliary verb and the subject. 'Nor did I' correctly matches the tense and logic.

questions.q: Rufta will study computer engineering at the university and ____.
why: To add a positive statement that applies to another person, we use 'So + auxiliary verb + subject'. Since the first clause uses 'will', the addition must also use 'will'.
